paragraphs.text: Chapter Six: A Familiar Den of Scum
Tatooine. Three months after the Battle of Endor.

Han Solo had never particularly liked Tatooine. It was hot, dusty, lawless, and populated by an extraordinary number of people who either wanted to kill him or collect money from him. Unfortunately, it was also one of the few places in the galaxy where he felt entirely at home.
"Coming up on Mos Eisley," he announced.
Chewbacca growled from the copilot's seat.
"Of course I remember what happened last time."
The Wookiee barked something considerably louder.
"All right, maybe some of it was my fault."

The Millennium Falcon descended through the planet's upper atmosphere, its battered hull shuddering as the desert winds caught it. Below them stretched an endless expanse of orange sand. Two suns hung low over the horizon. Han glanced toward the passenger seat. He could almost imagine Luke sitting there, barely more than a kid, staring out at the landscape he had been so desperate to escape. That had been only four years ago. Four years. It seemed impossible.

Back then, Han had been concerned primarily with paying off Jabba the Hutt, keeping the Falcon operational, and avoiding Imperial patrols. Now Jabba was dead, the Emperor was dead, and Han Solo was a celebrated general of the Rebel Alliance. He still owed money to several people on Tatooine. Some things, apparently, were beyond the reach of galactic revolution.

The cantina was almost exactly as he remembered it. Dim lighting. Low ceilings. Music drifting from the far end of the room. And the unmistakable smell of cheap liquor, overheated machinery, and several species whose personal hygiene practices Han had never understood. He stepped through the entrance with Chewbacca close behind. The music stopped. A dozen heads turned. Someone dropped a glass. Han sighed.
A blue-skinned Duros at the nearest table rose so quickly that his chair fell backward.
A Rodian near the bar muttered something to his companion. Another patron leaned forward.
"No," Han said. "That was a team effort."

By the time they reached the bar, half the cantina was watching them. Han found the attention irritating. He had spent years trying to remain unnoticed in places like this. Now complete strangers wanted to buy him drinks. Which, admittedly, was an improvement. The bartender, Wuher, stared at him from behind a row of battered containers.
"Thought you'd left the planet for good."
Wuher stopped polishing a glass. Han noticed.
"Then you probably know where the basement is."
"Listen to me, Solo. There are some parts of this place you don't want to go poking around in."
"Funny. That's exactly what people used to say about the Death Star."

Ten minutes later, Han and Chewbacca stood in a narrow storage room behind the bar. Wuher had reluctantly unlocked the door after Chewbacca explained, at considerable volume, that they were acting on behalf of the new galactic government. Han had then explained that Chewbacca's suggestion to remove the door entirely was not strictly necessary. The storage room contained crates, cleaning equipment, and a refrigerator that sounded as though it had been repaired by someone with a personal dislike of refrigeration.
At the back stood a metal panel. Han examined it.
"Yeah. Brand-new lock on a twenty-year-old door."

Han crouched beside it. The access mechanism was Imperial. Not the cheap equipment usually found in Mos Eisley. This was proper military hardware. Encrypted keypad. Independent power supply. Tamper detection.
"Somebody really didn't want customers wandering down here."
Chewbacca produced a small tool from his belt. Han glanced at him.
"You're not going to cut through the door?"
Chewbacca inserted the tool into the access panel. A shower of sparks erupted. The lock fell apart. Han stared.
"Technically, that counts as cutting through the door."
Chewbacca pushed it open. The tunnel beyond was surprisingly clean. No sand. No dust. No evidence of the desert settlement above. A row of recessed lights illuminated the floor. Han drew his blaster.

They followed the passage downward. After several turns, it opened into a circular chamber lined with communications equipment. Most of the instruments were old. Some appeared to date back to the Clone Wars. But several had been replaced recently. Chewbacca examined a console and growled.
"Yeah," Han said. "Somebody's been keeping this place running."

At the center of the room stood a recording terminal. Its display remained active. A list of dates filled the screen. Han scrolled through them. The entries went back decades. Merchant conversations. Smuggling transactions. Docking clearances. Bounty contracts. Ordinary cantina gossip.
"The Emperor was listening to this dump."
"Yeah, I know. Apparently he had nothing better to do."

Han opened a random recording. A hologram appeared. The cantina. Fifteen years earlier. A group of smugglers argued over shipping tariffs. Nothing unusual. He selected another. Two Imperial officers discussed a missing shipment of weapons. Another. A frightened merchant offered a bribe to a customs inspector. Han shook his head.
"Half the people in this place were breaking the law."
Chewbacca gave him a long look.
He continued searching. Then a familiar name caught his eye. SOLO, HAN — FREIGHT CAPTAIN. Han stopped.

Chewbacca leaned closer. A photograph appeared. Han himself. Younger. Smirking. Wearing the same vest he still owned. Beneath the photograph was a short assessment. Independent freighter captain. Questionable reliability. Significant financial liabilities. Likely to encounter fatal difficulties within one standard year. Han stared at the final sentence.
Chewbacca laughed so hard he had to grip the console.

Han opened the attached file. A recording began. The cantina, four years earlier. He recognized the date. The day he had met Luke Skywalker and Obi-Wan Kenobi. The hologram showed his younger self seated at a table with the old Jedi and a nervous farm boy. Han felt an unexpected pang of nostalgia. Old Ben. He had almost forgotten how the man looked. The gray beard. The hooded robe. The infuriating calm with which he had discussed impossible things.
A good man, Han now understood. A man who had given his life to help them escape. The recording was silent. Han frowned. He increased the audio level. Nothing.
Chewbacca examined the terminal. A short growl.
The Wookiee tapped several controls. A burst of static filled the room. Then voices. Han's own voice, younger and more arrogant. He winced.

The recording continued. Old Ben discussed transportation to Alderaan. Luke sat beside him, looking as though he had never been inside a room containing so many dangerous people. Han watched for a moment. Then he noticed something. A small red symbol flashed beside Obi-Wan's image. SUBJECT IDENTIFIED — RETROSPECTIVE ANALYSIS. He opened the notation. An Imperial intelligence report appeared. Possible surviving Jedi. Voice and facial characteristics consistent with General Obi-Wan Kenobi. Identification added following the Battle of Yavin.
"So they didn't know who he was at the time."
"Yeah. Somebody went through these recordings afterward."

He studied the date. The identification had been added weeks after Luke destroyed the first Death Star. Palpatine's agents had been searching backward through old surveillance records, trying to understand how the boy from Tatooine had reached the Rebellion. Han found that unsettling. The Emperor had been dead for three months. But his intelligence machinery had spent decades collecting fragments of people's lives. Fragments that could be assembled long after the people themselves had forgotten the conversations.

The next discovery was less amusing. A collection of transport records occupied a separate section of the archive. Most concerned ordinary Imperial cargo shipments. But several had been marked with a designation Han recognized from Leia's briefing. AUREL SEVEN. Forty-three prisoners. Alderaanian origin. He opened the earliest entry. A shipment had arrived on Tatooine several years before Alderaan's destruction. Not the prisoners themselves. Medical supplies. Restraint equipment. Specialized recording devices.

And a series of memory-storage components whose purpose Han did not understand. The receiving authority was listed as an Imperial research office. No name. No location beyond the cantina's underground station. Chewbacca growled quietly.
Han opened another file. This one contained a voice recording. A man spoke in formal, precise Basic.
"Transfer authorization confirmed. Aurel Seven subjects are to remain isolated from all civilian traffic. No correspondence. No unauthorized visitors."
The voice sounded familiar. Han listened again. Then frowned.
"Does that sound like somebody we know?"
Chewbacca listened. His expression changed. A low growl escaped him.

The voice sounded like the captain who had welcomed Leia to the Imperial Palace. Darren. But the recording was years old. Long before Darren's apparent suicide. Han checked the file. The speaker was not identified. Only a reference number appeared. VOICE PROFILE 044. He opened the accompanying information. Original sample acquired: Imperial year fourteen. Reconstruction quality: 98.7 percent. Authorized use: Witness conditioning. Han stared at the screen.
"Looks like it isn't necessarily the real guy talking."

Han played the recording again. The voice was perfect. The accent. The pauses. Even the slight roughness in the final syllables. He understood why Leia had been so disturbed by the interrogation recording. Someone had built a machine capable of making a person appear to say things they had never said. And that machine had been operating for years. He copied the files onto a portable data cylinder.
"Leia's going to want to see this."

Then he noticed another entry. A recent one. Very recent. Six days earlier. The same day the Emperor's private chamber on Coruscant had been accessed. The file had been opened remotely. The authorization belonged to one of Palpatine's advisers. SIM ALOO. Han frowned. That name had appeared in the Emperor's personal records. One of the strange men who had accompanied him to the second Death Star. A man presumed dead. Yet someone was still using his credentials.

Han opened the access history. Only one file had been retrieved. SUBJECT 044 — EMERGENCY ACTIVATION. He examined the attached transmission. A short command. Encoded. Destination: Coruscant. Time of delivery: the morning Darren had jumped. Han felt a cold sensation settle in his stomach.
"I think we just found out what set Darren off."
A sharp metallic click sounded behind them. Han turned. At the entrance stood a security droid. Tall. Black. Armed. Its single red optical sensor moved between them.
"Yeah, well, we're kind of authorized now."

The droid raised its weapon. Han fired first. The blaster bolt struck its shoulder, spinning it sideways. Chewbacca roared and charged. The droid fired. A red bolt struck the ceiling. Han ducked behind the console.

Chewbacca seized the droid by one arm and slammed it against the wall. Its weapon clattered across the floor. The machine attempted to strike him with its remaining arm. Chewbacca tore the arm free. Han emerged from behind the console.
The droid's head separated from its body. It bounced twice and rolled across the floor. Chewbacca stood over the wreckage, breathing heavily. Han looked at the destroyed machine. Then at his friend.
A second click sounded. Then another. Somewhere deeper in the facility, machinery began moving. Han looked toward the corridor.
A warning light illuminated above the door. SECURITY PURGE INITIATED. He groaned.
"Does every Imperial secret room do that?"
They ran. They emerged into the cantina storage room just as the underground security shutters slammed shut behind them. Wuher stared at the smoking access panel. Then at Chewbacca. Then at Han.
"I told you not to go down there!"
"Yeah, well, you forgot to mention the killer droids."
Chewbacca gave a pleased rumble. Wuher closed his eyes.
Back aboard the Falcon, Han transmitted the recovered records to Leia through an encrypted Alliance channel. He waited while the connection established. Her hologram appeared above the console.
"Found your secret station. Found some recordings. Nearly got killed by a security droid."
A satisfied growl came from the copilot's seat.
"Listen, sweetheart. We found something about Darren."
"Someone sent an activation command from this station to Coruscant on the morning he jumped."
"That's the interesting part. The authorization belonged to Sim Aloo."
"But he died aboard the second Death Star."
"There's something else. The station was recording people for years. Voices, conversations, all kinds of things. Somebody's been using those recordings to manufacture commands."
"Not yet. Most of the records are encrypted."
"Han, I want you to bring those files back."
"We can send a proper intelligence team later. Those records may explain what happened to Darren."
Han considered arguing. Then he saw her face.
"Don't thank me yet. I haven't sent you the bill."

The hologram vanished. Han leaned back. For a moment, he stared at the data cylinder resting beside the controls. An entire secret Imperial operation beneath a cantina. Recordings of conversations from years ago. Someone using the voice of a dead Emperor's adviser to activate a command inside another man's mind. He shook his head.
"Yeah. Smuggling spice. Dodging customs. Running away from people who wanted to kill us."

He started the engines. Outside, the twin suns were sinking toward the horizon. The Falcon lifted from the landing bay and climbed into the orange sky. Han activated the navigation computer. Then his console chimed. An incoming message. Not from Leia. Not from Alliance command. It came from an unknown transmitter somewhere in Mos Eisley. The screen displayed a single sentence. GENERAL SOLO. THE EMPEROR IS DEAD. HIS ORDERS ARE NOT. Han stared at it.

The Wookiee leaned over. Han read the message aloud. Then a second line appeared. YOU HAVE TAKEN SOMETHING THAT DOES NOT BELONG TO YOU. A third. RETURN THE RECORDS, OR THE NEXT VOICE YOU HEAR MAY BE YOUR OWN. The message vanished. Han looked at Chewbacca. For once, neither of them had anything to say.
